lines.note: Continues f330's monogonomi entry with monogonomina and a phrase for a person who likes varied or curious things. The second form has no securely printed long-o mark; the OCR's mǒnogonomi is not retained.

Hito completes the preceding Japanese phrase, translated as curious or inquisitive. The OCR borrowed Cada couſa, ou from the next row; that duplicate is removed here and remains fully represented in c1-l003.
Monogoto and monogotoni mean each thing and in each thing. This independent entry starts at the column margin.
Completes the distributive explanation. The OCR's attached Metendoſe no belongs to c1-l005, where it is retained; no printed material is lost by removing that duplicate here.
Monogoshi ni means with something intervening, paraphrased by hedatete. The Portuguese begins a description of an object placed between observer and target.

runs.text: meo algũa couſa, como parede, grades, &c.

lines.note: The intervening object may be a wall, bars, or similar barrier. The printed meo is preserved rather than modernized to meio.

Monogoshi ni nanzo wo kiku means hearing something through an intervening barrier. The damaged sequence is provisionally read nanzouo qiqu from its remaining rounded types and Japanese construction, replacing the OCR's unparseable nanzqumqiqu; the vowel after z remains a caveat.

runs.text: algũa couſa metendoſe no meo parede, taboa,

lines.note: Continues the translation of hearing something with a wall or board in between. The physical row remains separate although the sentence runs on.
Introduces seeing through or past an intervening object. The scan supports the g in Monogoxini, not the OCR's p.

runs.text: antre algũa couſa que està no meo.

lines.note: Completes the seeing example with something situated in between. The historical antre and grave in està are retained.
Monogurui denotes a mad person or madness in this gloss. The example begins becoming mad and continues naru below.
Completes monogurui ni naru, to become mad. Endoudecer is the printed Portuguese verb and is not modernized.

Monoguruuaxij describes being mad or behaving like a mad person. After the NINJAL lexical check prompted reinspection, enlargement clearly resolves two successive u-types after r; both are retained, rather than the first pass's mistaken simplification. The Portuguese continues below.
Completes the comparison with a mad person. This short gloss continuation is indented rather than a new headword.

This is the nominal derivative for madness or mad behaviour. Enlarged comparison with the adjective above confirms two u-types after r and a long ſ in the ending; the short derivative row stays indented.
This is the adverbial derivative of the same adjective. The scan confirms the doubled u sequence after r and a downward-pointing caron over final u; neither is simplified.

runs.text: O que falla, ou pratica bẽ. ¶

lines.note: Monoii is someone who speaks or converses well. The last abbreviated word is bẽ, not OCR tẽ; Mo- begins the further example below.
Monoiigoto ga aru means that talk or discussion is current. The Portuguese begins the explanation of such circulating talk.
The talk may concern an uprising, war, and similar matters. This qualifies the preceding expression rather than narrowing every use of monoii to military discussion.
Monoimi is explained through ominous or taboo observances. The printed space in the headword is retained; ji- begins jibun, a time or period.

runs.text: Tempo em que os gentios tem por a-

lines.note: Jibun completes the Japanese phrase for a period of abstention. The Portuguese describes a time when the people called gentios by the dictionary regard an act as inauspicious.

runs.text: gouro fazer algũa couſa, como ir diante do

lines.note: Completes agouro and gives approaching a kami as an example of the avoided action. The embedded Japanese Ca- is kept in its locally upright type and continues on the next row.

runs.text: , &c. por reſpeito da morte dalguem, ou

lines.note: Mi completes Cami. The abstention is associated with someone's death or another circumstance; reſpeito corrects OCR veſpeito, without endorsing the dictionary's description as a universal rule.
Completes the alternative explanation for the observance. This is continuous Portuguese prose attached to monoimi.

runs.text: Couſa pera ver, ou apraziuel à vi-

lines.note: Monomi first denotes something worth seeing or pleasing to the eye. The Portuguese divides vista at the physical line boundary.
Monomina koto exemplifies something to see. The final stop after ver is visible and restored; ſta completes the previous row's vista.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Ianelinha, ou fresta por onde ſe ve

lines.note: A second meaning is a small window or slit through which one sees. The paragraph sign omitted by OCR is restored at the start of this physical row.
Specifies looking from inside a litter, carriage, or similar conveyance. This completes the viewing-aperture sense of monomi.

runs.text: Modo de chamar à porta, como

lines.note: Monomoo is a formula for calling at a door. The long-o caron is visible; the Portuguese comparison continues below.
Completes the comparison with a call equivalent to hallo. The printed oula is retained rather than replaced by a modern Portuguese greeting.
Monomonoshii describes an imposing person, exemplified by a well-equipped soldier. The source's description concerns bearing and outward appearance.
Continues the image of someone well arranged or equipped, whose outward appearance suggests capability. The final conjunction belongs to the next row's description of manner.
Completes the impression that the person will perform notable feats. The cedilla in façanhas is visible; Monomono- starts the next example.

runs.text: Modo, ou aparencia de peßoa que

lines.note: Monomonoshii tei describes an imposing manner or appearance. The gap before t is very narrow; joined xijtei is provisionally retained in agreement with the aligned draft, while its grammatical components are distinguished only in this note.
The person has spirit or mettle and arms himself well. This completes the outward-bearing example rather than defining a separate military rank.
Mono no hon is a written notebook or book. The historical h-row spelling fon and Portuguese liuro are retained.
Mononofu denotes warriors or soldiers. The Portuguese gives the plural soldados directly.
Mononogu here means arms or military equipment. It is a separate entry from the similar-looking expression about a frightened horse that follows.
This expression describes a horse taking fright. Its printed Mononogu is retained even though the associated meaning differs from the preceding arms entry.

runs.text: com algum ſom, ou estrondo q̃ ouue. ¶

lines.note: The horse is startled by a sound or crash it hears. The abbreviation q̃ is preserved, and Mo- starts the example repeated on the next row.
Completes the expression for a horse that startles at noise. The Portuguese adjective continues after the abbreviated nasal syllable.

runs.text: tadiço do ſom, ou voz q̃ ouue.

lines.note: Completes the description of sensitivity to a sound or voice. The scan has ouue with two u types, correcting the draft's oue.

Mono ni osowaruru describes being overcome by something in a dream. Denoite is the closely set Portuguese night-time expression, not OCR dencite; the account continues with fear and inability to speak.

runs.text: com medo dalgũa couſa ſem poder falar, co-

lines.note: The dreamer is afraid of something and cannot speak. Co- begins the comparison completed below; this describes the dictionary's experience-label, not a modern medical diagnosis.

runs.text: mo quem eſtà com o peſadelo.

lines.note: Completes the comparison with someone suffering a nightmare. The wording ties the preceding fear and speechlessness to the dictionary's pesadelo gloss.

Mononoke is described as a demon, fox, or similar agency. The Japanese headword and Demonio correct the OCR's letter and spacing errors; the faint short terminal stroke is provisionally retained as a hyphen.

runs.text: lhante que dizem estar no corpo de hum en-

lines.note: The source explicitly says that such an agency is said to be in the body of a possessed person. The scan supports dizem, corpo, and hum; en- continues the final Portuguese word below.

Completes endemoninhado. Enlargement shows the weak n before h; the historical nh spelling is retained rather than replaced with modern endemoniado. This last body row is distinct from the lower page rule.
Mono no waza is glossed as the work of the devil. This records the dictionary's religious interpretation, not an independent claim about supernatural causation.
Mono kire denotes a very sharp-cutting sword. The printed space in the Japanese expression and the Portuguese spelling Catana are retained.
Monosabita describes a lonely place formerly inhabited. Its explanation continues with what has become of that settlement.
Completes the description of a place left deserted and ruined. The worn deſerto is read as one word, not the OCR's de ſerto; the row is visibly a continuation.
Monosabishii is given the same meaning as the preceding lonely or deserted-place description. Idem is printed italic.
The corresponding noun denotes that loneliness or desolation. Its isolated indented presentation is retained without inventing a missing gloss.
The adverbial derivative has a marked long u. The scan supports the retained caron-shaped mark.
Monosashi is a measure or measuring implement compared to a cubit. The use in garment cutting is specified on the next rows.

runs.text: medir pano, cangas, &c. quando talhão algũ

lines.note: The measure is used for cloth and the other named textile material while cutting clothing. The abbreviated algũ is retained rather than expanded.
Completes the garment-making explanation. This short word is a body continuation, not furniture.
Monosugoi is glossed as something solitary and frightening. Me- continues into medo on the next row.

runs.text: do, como hum mato grande, & ſolitario.

lines.note: Completes medo and gives a large, lonely wood as the example. This historical gloss emphasizes eeriness rather than imposing a modern broad intensifier sense.
Monotachigatana is an iron cutting implement. The definition continues with its broad blade and use in cutting garments.

runs.text: ro, como faca larga com que cortão de vestir.

lines.note: Completes ferro and compares the implement to a broad knife used for clothing work. The historical de vestir construction is preserved.
Monotsukuri here denotes a farmer skilled at cultivation. The damaged Portuguese adjective reads bem, correcting OCR hem.

runs.text: campos, ou varzeas. Palaura vſada em al-

lines.note: The objects of cultivation are fields or low-lying agricultural lands. The sentence then begins a regional usage restriction, continued below.

runs.text: gũas partes do Cami entre os lauradores.

lines.note: Completes the regional restriction: the word is used among farmers in some parts of Cami. Cami is an embedded Japanese regional designation, but its locally italic printing is retained.

runs.text: Couſa ridiculoſa, ou de que ſe po

lines.note: Monowarai denotes something laughable or mockable. The divided po/de has no securely visible terminal hyphen here, so none is supplied.
Completes poder rir e zombar, then begins becoming an object of ridicule. The faint i of Monovaraini is restored from the visible trace and the noun above, rather than retaining OCR Monovara ni.

runs.text: Dar occaſião de ſe rirem, & moteja-

lines.note: Naru completes the Japanese example. Its Portuguese explanation is giving others occasion to laugh at and mock someone.
Completes motejarem delle, mocking him. The short row belongs to the previous example and remains indented.
Monouchi is exemplified by the striking or cutting portion of a sword. Par- begins parte in the Portuguese definition below.

runs.text: te dianteira da Catana do meo por diante com

lines.note: The relevant portion is described as the forward part of the sword, from its middle onward. The source's wording is retained without imposing a modern measured boundary.
Completes the description as the part normally used for cutting. The doubled consonants in commummente follow the print.
Monouchidokoro is given as equivalent to monouchi. The printed l introduces the alternate form and Idem links back to the preceding definition.
Monoui describes something sad, painful, or miserable. The scan gives triste and penoſa, with an intervening ampersand, rather than the OCR's trißa and penodſa.
Completes miserauel, the final Portuguese equivalent. Its physical separation is preserved.
Monouu is the corresponding adverbial form. The marked u is retained without converting the historical spelling to a modern form.
Monousa is the noun corresponding to monoui. The printed v represents the same u-like material but remains v in the transcription.
Mono-odoroki suru introduces the action of taking fright. In the repetition, the weak rounded vowel is read o with support from its remaining outline and the headword, not OCR e.

runs.text: Eſpantarſe o homem, ou caualo quando cami-

lines.note: The explanation applies to a person or horse being startled while traveling or walking. Cami- continues into caminha below. The faint short terminal mark near the rule is provisionally retained as a hyphen.
Completes caminha and closes the example. This is an ordinary short continuation, not a missing new entry.
Monookidokoro is a place where something is put or kept. The printed vo spelling is retained rather than modernized.
Completes the definition of a storage or placement location. The tilde remains on u in algũa.

runs.text: Monouo mi, iru, ita. Monouo miru vma.

lines.note: Gives the principal forms of mono wo miru and repeats the horse expression. The special shying sense is resolved by the cross-reference on the next row.
The Portuguese instruction directs the reader to Mono, where f330 explains a horse suddenly taking fright. Mono is a lexical reference embedded in the Portuguese apparatus, not a new headword here.
Monowosomi suru is exemplified as taking fright. Vt and ſuru correct the OCR's Vs and ſi ru; the abbreviated Portuguese form continues below.
Completes the startled-state gloss and adds an upright regional X. label. Particularmen- is a single divided word, not the OCR's separated fragments.
Completes particularmente and specifies that the expression is especially said of a horse. This is a usage qualification, not another animal name.

runs.text: O eſpantarſe homem, ou o ca-

lines.note: A closely related headword covers a person or horse taking fright. Ca- begins caualo at the line boundary.
Completes caualo and gives the verbal example. Monouozomi corrects the OCR's internal u/n confusion; Idẽ ends in a stop, not a hyphen anticipating another row.
Monoshiri denotes a learned person. The headword starts at the column margin, correcting the provisional continuation indentation.
Monoyoshi is presented as a euphemistic term for a person with leprosy. The historical terms are retained as source wording; the register restriction follows below.

runs.text: molheres. Vſa ſe tambem entre outra gete par-

lines.note: The dictionary first labels it women's speech, then says others also use it. The defective or abbreviated-looking gete is retained without supplying an unseen n; par- continues into particularmente.

runs.text: ticularmente no tempo de Xǒguachi, &c. em

lines.note: The usage is associated particularly with the New Year period. Enlargement supports the caron in Xǒguachi and a faint remnant of c before h; this worn embedded Japanese word is retained as a nonblocking caveat.

The dictionary supplies Facuyoxi as the expression used in other places. The worn x retains a small crossing remnant; it is not the OCR's a. This is a Japanese term within a Portuguese regional explanation.

Monozuki denotes a curious person who enjoys the activities continued on f332. The scan supports zuqi and curioſa, correcting the malformed draft headword and vowel; the separate fazer catchword anticipates the next page.
The italic catchword fazer anticipates the first body word of f332. The OCR had merged it with the separate gathering signature T t 2 to its left; both printed items are now recorded separately.
